## Proposition 12.11
**Statement:** Cones and cylinders which are of the same height are to one another as their bases.

**Step 1.** Let C₁ and C₂ be cones of equal height, with circular bases of areas B₁ and B₂. We first prove C₁:C₂ = B₁:B₂ by exhaustion with inscribed polygonal pyramids. The polygonal-pyramid theorem is the direct choice, since it avoids triangulating the inscribed bases [12.6]. We will then obtain the assertion for cylinders from the cone–cylinder relation [12.10].

**Step 2.** Through the centre of each base draw two perpendicular diameters. Successively bisect every angle between adjacent radii, extend the bisectors to the circumference, and join consecutive circumference points [1.11, P2, 1.9, P1]. Perform the same number of subdivisions in both circles. Corresponding central angles are initially equal right angles and remain equal under bisection [P4, 1.9]. The central triangles are isosceles, because their two radial sides are equal; corresponding central triangles are therefore equiangular [D1.15, 1.5, 1.32]. Their corresponding sides are proportional [6.4]. Consequently, the corresponding polygonal sides are proportional, and the corresponding polygonal angles, being sums of corresponding triangle angles, are equal [CN2]. Thus the two polygons at every common stage are similar [D6.1].

**Step 3.** At any common stage, denote the polygonal areas by F₁ and F₂, and join their vertices to the respective cone vertices to obtain inscribed pyramids P₁ and P₂ [P1, 3.2, D11.12, D11.18]. The ratios F₁:F₂ and B₁:B₂ both equal the ratio of the squares on the base diameters [12.1, 12.2]; hence F₁:F₂ = B₁:B₂ [5.11]. Since the pyramids have equal height,
P₁:P₂ = F₁:F₂ = B₁:B₂ [12.6, 5.11].

**Step 4.** We show that these pyramids exhaust their cones. In either base let AB be a current polygonal side, O the centre, and M the new circumference point introduced between A and B by the next angular bisection. Let N be the intersection of OM with AB. Since OA = OB and OM bisects angle AOB, triangles OAN and OBN are congruent; therefore OM is perpendicular to AB [D1.15, 1.4, D1.10]. Construct the rectangle R with base AB, on the side towards M, whose opposite side passes through M [1.11, 1.31, 1.29]. That opposite side is perpendicular to OM and therefore supports the circle at M [3.16]. The perpendiculars at A and B also bound the circular segment: since the arc AB is at most a quadrant, a point on the arc side of AB and beyond either endpoint perpendicular would have perpendicular distances from the two lines ON and AB making its distance from O greater than OA, by the right-triangle square relation [1.47, CN5]. Such a point cannot belong to the circular disk [D1.15]. Thus the circular segment bounded by AB and its minor arc is a proper part of R.

**Step 5.** Let W be the solid formed by joining the cone vertex to that circular segment, and let T and Q be the pyramids with the same vertex and respective bases triangle AMB and rectangle R [D11.18, D11.12]. The rectangle is twice triangle AMB, since they have the same base and lie between the same parallels [1.41]. Hence Q = 2T by the equal-height pyramid theorem [12.6, D5.5]. But W is a proper part of Q, so W < 2T [CN5]. Adding M to the polygon removes T from W; thus it removes more than half of W. Applying this to every current side and adding the removed parts shows that each refinement removes more than half of the entire remainder between the cone and its inscribed pyramid [CN2, CN3].

**Step 6.** Consequently, the remainder Cᵢ − Pᵢ can be made smaller than any assigned positive solid magnitude [10.1]. More generally, for any fixed positive integer k, the successive magnitudes k(Cᵢ − Pᵢ) also decrease by more than half, so they too can be made smaller than any assigned positive solid magnitude [CN2, 10.1]. Refinement is always performed in both circles together, preserving the proportion established in Step 3.

**Step 7.** We verify the required proportion by the definition of equal ratios. Fix arbitrary positive integers m and n [D5.5]. First suppose mB₁ = nB₂. Step 3 then gives mP₁ = nP₂ at every common stage [D5.5]. If mC₁ > nC₂, put Δ = mC₁ − nC₂ and choose a stage with m(C₁ − P₁) < Δ [Step 6; 10.1]. Subtracting gives mP₁ > nC₂ > nP₂, a contradiction [CN3, CN5]. Interchanging the two cones likewise excludes mC₁ < nC₂. Therefore mC₁ = nC₂.

**Step 8.** Now suppose mB₁ > nB₂. Fix an initial common pair of inscribed pyramids P₁⁰ and P₂⁰. By Step 3 and the definition of equal ratios, mP₁⁰ > nP₂⁰; let δ = mP₁⁰ − nP₂⁰, a positive solid magnitude [D5.5]. For any strictly finer common pair P₁, P₂, both the whole pyramids and the subtracted initial pyramids have ratio B₁:B₂. Therefore
(P₁ − P₁⁰):(P₂ − P₂⁰) = B₁:B₂ [5.19, 5.11].
It follows that m(P₁ − P₁⁰) > n(P₂ − P₂⁰) [D5.5]. Adding the initial magnitudes gives
mP₁ > nP₂ + δ [CN2].

**Step 9.** Choose this finer common stage so that n(C₂ − P₂) < δ [Step 6; 10.1]. Then nC₂ < nP₂ + δ < mP₁ < mC₁ [CN2, CN5]. Thus mB₁ > nB₂ implies mC₁ > nC₂.

**Step 10.** Interchanging the two indices and the multipliers in Steps 8–9 shows that mB₁ < nB₂ implies mC₁ < nC₂. Together with Step 7, this proves that, for every pair of positive integers m,n, the multiples mC₁ and nC₂ have exactly the same comparison as mB₁ and nB₂. Therefore C₁:C₂ = B₁:B₂ [D5.5].

**Step 11.** Finally, let Z₁ and Z₂ be cylinders with bases B₁ and B₂ and the same height as the corresponding cones. Each cylinder is three times its cone [12.10]. Magnitudes have the same ratio as their equimultiples, so Z₁:Z₂ = C₁:C₂ [5.15]. Combining this with Step 10 yields Z₁:Z₂ = B₁:B₂ [5.11]. Hence cones of equal height are to one another as their bases, and cylinders of equal height are likewise to one another as their bases.

heath_proof_text: Let there be cones and cylinders of the same height, let the circles ABCD, EFGH be their bases, KL, MN their axes and AC, EG the diameters of their bases; I say that, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to the cone EN. For, if not, then, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so will the cone AL be either to some solid less than the cone EN or to a greater. First, let it be in that ratio to a less solid O, and let the solid X be equal to that by which the solid O is less than the cone EN; therefore the cone EN is equal to the solids O, X. Let the square EFGH be inscribed in the circle EFGH; therefore the square is greater than the half of the circle. Let there be set up from the square EFGH a pyramid of equal height with the cone; therefore the pyramid so set up is greater than the half of the cone, inasmuch as, if we circumscribe a square about the circle, and set up from it a pyramid of equal height with the cone, the inscribed pyramid is half of the circumscribed pyramid, for they are to one another as their bases, [XII. 6] while the cone is less than the circumscribed pyramid. Let the circumferences EF, FG, GH, HE be bisected at the points P, Q, R, S, and let HP, PE, EQ, QF, FR, RG, GS, SH be joined. Therefore each of the triangles HPE, EQF, FRG, GSH is greater than the half of that segment of the circle which is about it. On each of the triangles HPE, EQF, FRG, GSH let there be set up a pyramid of equal height with the cone; therefore, also, each of the pyramids so set up is greater than the half of that segment of the cone which is about it. Thus, bisecting the circumferences which are left, joining straight lines, setting up on each of the triangles pyramids of equal height with the cone, and doing this continually, we shall leave some segments of the cone which will be less than the solid X. [X. 1] Let such be left, and let them be the segments on HP, PE, EQ, QF, FR, RG, GS, SH; therefore the remainder, the pyramid of which the polygon HPEQFRGS is the base and the height the same with that of the cone, is greater than the solid O. Let there also be inscribed in the circle ABCD the polygon DTAUBVCW similar and similarly situated to the polygon HPEQFRGS, and on it let a pyramid be set up of equal height with the cone AL. Since then, as the square on AC is to the square on EG, so is the polygon DTAUBVCW to the polygon HPEQFRGS, [XII. 1] while, as the square on AC is to the square on EG, so is the circle ABCD to the circle EFGH, [XII. 2] therefore also, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the polygon DTAUBVCW to the polygon HPEQFRGS. But, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to the solid O, and, as the polygon DTAUBVCW is to the polygon HPEQFRGS, so is the pyramid of which the polygon DTAUBVCW is the base and the point L the vertex to the pyramid of which the polygon HPEQFRGS is the base and the point N the vertex. [XII. 6] Therefore also, as the cone AL is to the solid O, so is the pyramid of which the polygon DTAUBVCW is the base and the point L the vertex to the pyramid of which the polygon HPEQFRGS is the base and the point N the vertex; [V. 11] therefore, alternately, as the cone AL is to the pyramid in it, so is the solid O to the pyramid in the cone EN. [V. 16] But the cone AL is greater than the pyramid in it; therefore the solid O is also greater than the pyramid in the cone EN. But it is also less: which is absurd. Therefore the cone AL is not to any solid less than the cone EN as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH. Similarly we can prove that neither is the cone EN to any solid less than the cone AL as the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD. I say next that neither is the cone AL to any solid greater than the cone EN as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH. For, if possible, let it be in that ratio to a greater solid O; therefore, inversely, as the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD, so is the solid O to the cone AL. But, as the solid O is to the cone AL, so is the cone EN to some solid less than the cone AL; therefore also, as the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD, so is the cone EN to some solid less than the cone AL: which was proved impossible. Therefore the cone AL is not to any solid greater than the cone EN as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH. But it was proved that neither is it in this ratio to a less solid; therefore, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to the cone EN. But, as the cone is to the cone, so is the cylinder to the cylinder, for each is triple of each; [XII. 10] Therefore also, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so are the cylinders on them which are of equal height.
